title: The word Pope Francis kept saying

card.keepWhy: Mercy is received first, then given away.
sources: Matthew 9:9-13 (Jesus saw a man sitting in the custom house, named Matthew, and said, “Follow me”; he arose and followed him; many publicans and sinners sat down with Jesus; the Pharisees asked, “Why doth your master eat with publicans and sinners?”; “They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill. Go then and learn what this meaneth, I will have mercy and not sacrifice”). Douay-Rheims. Hosea 6:6. Parallels: Mark 2:13-17, Luke 5:27-32 (Levi makes him a great feast in his own house).
Bede, Homily 21 (Book I) on Saint Matthew, read in the Office of Readings on 21 September: “Vidit ergo Iesus publicanum, et quia miserando atque eligendo vidit, ait illi: Sequere me.”

Pope Francis: episcopal and papal motto “miserando atque eligendo”; interview with Antonio Spadaro, La Civiltà Cattolica, 2013 (“I am a sinner whom the Lord has looked upon”); confession at the Basilica of San José de Flores, Buenos Aires, 21 September 1953, which he described as the moment of his call. Misericordiae Vultus (2015), the Extraordinary Jubilee of Mercy 2015-2016.
Latin misericordia (miser, wretched + cor, heart). Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (the corporal and spiritual works of mercy), 1422-1424 (confession).
check: Matthew 9:10 says only “in the house”; Luke 5:29 makes it Levi’s own house. The caption says “Matthew’s house”. Confirm.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there something you haven’t quite forgiven yourself for?
options: i’m sorry you’re carrying it. this story is for you.
most of us have a pocket full. watch this look.

steps.line: In the lakeside town of Capernaum sat a tax collector named Matthew, taking money for Rome. People saw men like him as traitors and cheats.
One day Jesus walked past his table, looked straight at him, and said two words: “Follow me.”

steps.q: A man the whole town despises hears “Follow me.” What does Matthew do?
o: Asks for a day to think it over
Gets up and follows, right then
Says he must first pay back what he took
steps.why: He got up and followed. The Gospel tells it in a single line.

steps.line: Matthew got up from his table, left it all behind, and followed him.
Soon Matthew’s house was full: tax collectors and sinners at dinner with Jesus. Some religious men grumbled, “Why does he eat with people like them?”

steps.q: To the grumblers Jesus says, “It’s not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.” Who does that make the grumblers?
o: The real doctors in the story
People who think they don’t need one
People Jesus has given up on
steps.why: A gentle sting: no one is outside the clinic, only those who think they are. Then he quotes Hosea: “I desire mercy, not sacrifice.”

steps.line: Centuries later, an English monk named Bede wrote about that moment: Jesus looked at Matthew with mercy, and chose him.
steps.label: centuries later

steps.q: In Caravaggio’s famous painting of this calling, Jesus points into a dim room of tax collectors. Art lovers still argue about one thing. What?
o: Whether Jesus is even in it
Whether it shows day or night
steps.why: Some see the bearded man pointing at himself, “Me?” Others see the young man still counting coins. Pope Francis said of that pointing finger: that’s me.

steps.line: In 1953, a sixteen-year-old in Buenos Aires walked into a church on Saint Matthew’s day, went to confession, and felt that same look. He became Pope Francis.
steps.label: much later

steps.q: Misericordia, Latin for mercy, joins two words. Which?
steps.why: Miser, wretched, and cor, heart: a heart that goes out to someone in misery. Pope Francis took Bede’s line, miserando atque eligendo, as his motto.

say: here’s what i love. jesus didn’t wait for matthew to become a better man. he looked at him with mercy first, and the change came after.
pope francis kept saying it: you can’t give mercy you’ve never received. catholics receive it in confession, then give it away in the works of mercy: feeding, forgiving, visiting.

steps.q: Asked who he was, Pope Francis said: “a sinner the Lord has looked upon.” Why say that, not something grander?
o: He saw himself as Matthew, chosen by mercy
He was quoting a line from the Mass
He meant all popes are only priests
steps.why: His motto, by having mercy and by choosing, was his own story. He saw himself in the tax collector.

today.say: today, start with yourself. bring to mind the thing you haven’t forgiven yourself for, and picture someone who loves you looking at it, and at you, without flinching. then pass it on with one small work of mercy. if you pray, you can let that look be God’s.
options: good. let yourself be looked at kindly.
I’ll start with the small work
that works too. mercy often starts in the hands.
